newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew turn to sun to help damaged space station.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew turn to sun to help damaged space station.

text.p: The crew of the damaged Russian Mir space station have turned it to face the sun to help boost power supplies after a cargo craft collided with one of its science units, Itar-Tass news agency said on Thursday.
Tass, reporting from Mission Control near Moscow, said the Spektr science module's cooling system may have been broken in Wednesday's accident.
Officials said the crew, U.S. astronaut Michael Foale and Russian cosmonauts Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, were in no immediate danger.
"The crew on board Mir changed its position back to face the sun to supply the necessary boost to the electrical supply's buffer batteries after the accident," Tass said.
In Wednesday's collision, an unmanned Progress cargo craft bumped into the Spektr module, damaging one of four solar panels and robbing the entire station of up to half its energy supply.
Tass said the cooling system in that part of the station, now sealed off from the rest of the sprawling complex to stop a drop in air pressure, could also be damaged.

Officials said late on Wednesday the crew may have to go on an unscheduled space walk to inspect the damage caused in the incident, described by Mission Control as one of the worst Mir has experienced in the 11 years it has been in orbit.
The incident has raised fresh doubts about the safety of Moscow's space programme.

The chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives Science Committee, James Sensenbrenner, urged the American space agency NASA on Wednesday to begin a safety review of the Mir before any more U.S. astronauts went on board for a long-term stay.

The head of the Russian Mission Control, Vladimir Lobachyov, told a news conference on Wednesday that the Progress had punctured the scientific module and may have damaged one of the solar batteries, creating energy problems.

"The cosmonauts say there is a fall in the electrical supply ... and as a result of the collision a hole (in the scientific module used for the docking) has developed whose size is still unclear," he said.
A NASA spokesman said the crew had been able to seal off the damaged compartment.

Russian officials said the crew had sufficient water and food on board. But Vladimir Solovyov, responsible for flight coordination, conceded that an eighth of the Mir station was temporarily out of action because of the collision.
Lobachyov said a special commission comprising officials and experts had been set up to consider the situation and work out recommendations.
